programme.title: Report from the North Pole
programme.desc: Climate change is melting the polar ice caps. A report from the North Pole about rising temperatures, shrinking glaciers, and what it means for polar bears and the planet. The first Earth Rock episode, part of the 2009 direct-to-video revival focused on environmental education.

programme.title: Mother Goose Melodies
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #16 (1931). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Interjections!
programme.desc: "Interjections! Show excitement! Or emotion! They're generally set apart from a sentence by an exclamation point, or by a comma when the feeling's not as strong." A rapid-fire series of dramatic vignettes — a kid getting a shot, finding a dollar, being surprised at a party — each punctuated by interjections (Darn! Wow! Ouch! Hey!). The energy is relentless and perfectly captures what interjections actually do: interrupt the flow with raw feeling. Part of Grammar Rock. Performed with breathless enthusiasm by Essra Mohawk.

programme.title: Krtek (The Little Mole)
programme.desc: Krtek finds a broken watch and attempts to fix it. Time, gears, and the mechanical world through the eyes of a creature who lives by the sun.

programme.title: Donald in Mathmagic Land
programme.desc: Donald Duck ventures into Mathmagic Land, a wondrous world where trees have square roots and rivers brim with numbers. From Pythagoras and ancient Greek geometry to the Golden Ratio in art and nature, Donald discovers that mathematics is everywhere — in music, games, architecture, and the natural world. Released June 26, 1959. Nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. One of the most popular educational films ever made, shown in schools for decades.

programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #11 (1930). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Ready or Not, Here I Come
programme.desc: A game of hide-and-seek teaches the fives times table. "Five, ten, fifteen, twenty — ready or not, here I come!" Counting by fives is the most natural skip-counting pattern (it mirrors how we read clocks and count coins), and this episode leans into that intuition. Part of Multiplication Rock. Sung with a playful energy that captures the excitement of the chase.

programme.title: Birds In The Spring
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #34 (1933). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Tyrannosaurus Debt
programme.desc: The national debt as a dinosaur that keeps growing and growing. Borrowing money to pay for things the country wants but cannot afford, and the interest that piles up. A surprisingly sophisticated topic for a kids show — the animation shows the debt-dinosaur stomping through Washington getting bigger with each budget cycle. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: The Skeleton Dance

programme.title: Unpack Your Adjectives
programme.desc: A girl goes on a camping trip and unpacks adjectives from her backpack to describe everything she encounters. Blossom Dearie returns with her whispery delivery, turning grammar into a nature hike. The camping frame makes abstract description concrete — you need adjectives to tell someone what the bear looked like. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: Springtime
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #03 (1929). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: The Tale of Mr. Morton
programme.desc: A shy man named Mr. Morton has a crush on his neighbor Pearl. Each verse advances his love story while teaching subject-predicate sentence structure. Written and performed by Jack Sheldon. The last Grammar Rock episode, produced during the 1993 revival — twenty years after the original run. Gentler and more narrative than the 1970s episodes, telling a complete short story through grammar lessons. Mr. Morton gets the girl.

programme.title: The Little Things We Do
programme.desc: Small daily actions that help the environment — turning off lights, recycling, using less water, walking instead of driving. The message: environmental stewardship starts with individual habits, not grand gestures. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.desc: A father-and-sons street vendor operation sells adverbs from a cart. Bob Dorough and his real-life sons performed this one together. programme.title: Three Is a Magic Number
programme.desc: The song that started it all. Bob Dorough wrote and performed this jazzy ode to the number three — "a man and a woman had a little baby, yes they did, they had three in the family" — as a demo to prove that kids could learn math through music. It worked. ABC greenlit the entire Schoolhouse Rock series on the strength of this single track. Premiered January 6, 1973, the first of the Multiplication Rock series. Teaches the threes times table through a dreamy, improvisational jazz vocal over simple animation of triangles, three-leaf clovers, and three-ring circuses.

programme.title: Midnight In A Toyshop
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #12 (1930). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Telegraph Line
programme.desc: The nervous system explained as a telegraph network. Your brain sends electrical signals through nerves to every part of your body, and sensory nerves send messages back — just like telegraph operators sending and receiving Morse code along wires. Samuel Morse meets neuroscience. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: Electricity, Electricity (Goodness)
programme.desc: The band Goodness covers Electricity, Electricity for the Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute compilation. A grunge-influenced take on the Science Rock classic. Part of the 2002 tribute album series.

programme.title: Fireworks
programme.desc: The Declaration of Independence and the Fourth of July. The Continental Congress debates, Jefferson writes, and the colonies declare independence from Britain. The title refers both to the celebratory fireworks and to the explosive political act itself. Released during the American Bicentennial. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: $7.50 Once a Week
programme.desc: A kid gets a weekly allowance and learns to budget it — needs versus wants, saving for bigger purchases, and the pain of running out before the week is over. The specific dollar amount dates the episode perfectly to the mid-1990s. Part of Money Rock.

programme.title: Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips: Number Cruncher
programme.desc: Computers are number crunchers — they do math faster than any human can. Mr. Chips demonstrates calculations, sorting, and data processing at speeds that amaze Scooter. The last of the Scooter Computer series. Part of Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips.

programme.title: Don't Be a Carbon Sasquatch
programme.desc: Carbon footprints — every action has an environmental cost measured in carbon emissions. Driving, flying, heating your house, even eating certain foods. A Carbon Sasquatch leaves giant footprints everywhere. The goal: shrink your footprint. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: Lullaby Land
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #38 (1933). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: A Noun Is a Person, Place, or Thing
programme.desc: The first Grammar Rock episode. "Well, every person you can know, and every place that you can go, and anything that you can show — you know they're nouns." Lynn Ahrens wrote the lyrics for this and most of the Grammar Rock series, bringing a Broadway sensibility to three-minute educational shorts. A straightforward, catchy definition song that drills the concept through rapid-fire examples. Premiered September 1973 on ABC.

programme.title: Winter

programme.title: Mother Necessity
programme.desc: American invention and innovation, from Ben Franklin to Thomas Edison to Alexander Graham Bell. Necessity is the mother of invention, and America has always been full of necessities. The cotton gin, the steamboat, the telephone, the light bulb — each invention animated as it springs from its creator's need. Part of America Rock. Performed by Essra Mohawk.

programme.title: Three Ring Government
programme.desc: The three branches of the U.S. government — executive, legislative, and judicial — explained as three rings of a circus, each performing its own act but all part of the same show. Checks and balances as circus acts. The ringmaster (the Constitution) keeps them all in line. A companion to the more famous "I'm Just a Bill," focusing on the structural framework rather than the legislative process. Part of America Rock. Performed by Jack Sheldon.

programme.title: The Trash Can Band
programme.desc: Recycling and reuse through music — a band that makes instruments out of trash. Cans become drums, bottles become flutes, junk becomes art. The message is that waste is a failure of imagination. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #36 (1933). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #52 (1935). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: The Body Machine
programme.desc: Your body is a machine that needs fuel (food), maintenance (exercise), and rest (sleep). The heart pumps, the lungs breathe, the stomach digests — all the major systems explained as mechanical processes in a biological factory. The animation cross-cuts between a real machine and the human body doing the same work. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: Broken Toys
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #58 (1935). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: My Hero, Zero
programme.desc: A love song to the number zero — the placeholder that makes our number system work. "My hero, zero, such a funny little hero, but till you came along we counted on our fingers and toes." Bob Dorough explains how zero as a placeholder lets you write ten, a hundred, a thousand, and beyond. Part of Multiplication Rock. The animation features a caped zero flying through cascading digits.

programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #30 (1932). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.sub-title: How the Little Mole Got His Trousers
programme.desc: The very first Krtek film. A little mole needs trousers and enlists the woodland creatures to help make a pair from flax — harvesting, spinning, weaving, and sewing. Won two Golden Lions at the 1957 Venice Film Festival. The only episode with spoken dialogue.

programme.title: Three Little Wolves
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #60 (1936). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: What To Do On A Date
Elbow Room
programme.desc: Manifest Destiny and westward expansion. Lewis and Clark, the Louisiana Purchase, the Oregon Trail, the Gold Rush — America pushing west because it needed elbow room. The song is catchy enough that you almost miss how it glosses over what westward expansion cost the people already living there. A time capsule of how the 1970s taught this history. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: The Old Mill
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #68 (1937). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Conjunction Junction
programme.desc: The most famous Schoolhouse Rock episode. A train conductor at Conjunction Junction hooks up boxcars labeled "and," "but," and "or" to demonstrate how conjunctions connect words, phrases, and clauses. "Conjunction Junction, what's your function? Hooking up words and phrases and clauses." Written and performed by Bob Dorough. The train metaphor is so perfectly matched to the concept — conjunctions literally couple things together — that it became the definitive example of the series' genius. Four-time Daytime Emmy winner. Part of Grammar Rock.

programme.title: Elmer Elephant
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #59 (1936). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: The Four-Legged Zoo
programme.desc: A visit to a zoo full of four-legged animals teaches the fours times table from a different angle. Complements "Elementary, My Dear" by reinforcing the same multiplication facts through animal counting — four legs on a horse, eight legs on two horses, and so on through the zoo. Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips: Introduction
programme.desc: The introduction to the Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips series — the 1980s addition to Schoolhouse Rock teaching kids about personal computers. Scooter is a skateboarding kid, Mr. Chips is a friendly computer. Together they explain the digital revolution to a generation that was about to live through it. The weakest era of Schoolhouse Rock by consensus, but historically fascinating as a time capsule of early computer literacy education.

programme.title: The Flying Mouse
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #46 (1934). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Interplanet Janet
programme.desc: A girl named Janet zooms through the solar system visiting each planet in order. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto — the whole tour set to a disco beat. One of the most popular Science Rock episodes, both for its earworm melody and for the sheer joy of its space animation. Pluto was still a planet. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Lynn Ahrens.

programme.title: The Tortoise And The Hare
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #49 (1935). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Save the Ocean
programme.desc: Ocean pollution and marine conservation. Plastic, oil spills, and runoff are killing marine life. The ocean covers 70% of the Earth and produces much of our oxygen. Part of Earth Rock.

programme.title: The Golden Touch
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #50 (1935). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Verb: That's What's Happening
programme.desc: A superhero called Verb flies through the city demonstrating action words. "I get my thing in action — VERB! To be, to sing, to feel, to live — VERB! That's what's happening." Zachary Sanders delivers the vocal with disco-era energy. The animation puts Verb in a cape, soaring over buildings while performing every action he names. One of the most beloved Grammar Rock episodes. Written by Bob Dorough.

programme.title: The Weather Show
programme.desc: How weather works — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and the water cycle. Sun heats the ocean, water evaporates, clouds form, rain falls, rivers flow back to the ocean, repeat. The last of the original Science Rock episodes, wrapping up the 1970s run with the biggest system of all: the atmosphere. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: I'm Just a Bill (Folk Implosion)
programme.desc: Folk Implosion (Lou Barlow of Dinosaur Jr/Sebadoh) covers the iconic civics lesson. A lo-fi indie rock version of the most famous Schoolhouse Rock song. Part of the 2002 Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute compilation.

programme.title: A Victim of Gravity
programme.desc: Newton's apple, falling objects, and the universal force that keeps us stuck to the Earth. The first Science Rock episode introduces gravity through a kid who keeps dropping things and wondering why everything falls down, never up. The animation visualizes gravitational pull as an invisible hand. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: Little Twelvetoes
programme.desc: An alien with twelve fingers and twelve toes lives on a planet where base-12 is natural. "Now if man had been born with six fingers on each hand, he'd also have twelve toes, or so the theory goes." Bob Dorough uses this sci-fi premise to teach the twelves times table while sneaking in a lesson about why we use base-10 (we have ten fingers) and how other number bases work. The most conceptually ambitious Multiplication Rock episode — it teaches multiplication AND number theory. Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: I Got Six
programme.desc: A funky soul number about the sixes times table. "I got six — that's all, and that's been my lucky number since I was very small." Grady Tate brings a warm, grooving vocal to the multiplication facts that feel the least intuitive to kids (6×7, 6×8, 6×9). Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: The Grasshopper And The Ants
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #42 (1934). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: I'm Gonna Send Your Vote to College
programme.desc: The Electoral College explained. Your vote goes to college — the Electoral College — where electors cast the actual ballots for President. A revival-era America Rock episode that tackles one of the most confusing parts of American democracy. The surround-sound remix suggests this is from a later home video release. Jack Sheldon returns to voice the befuddled voter trying to understand why his vote takes a detour through 538 electors.

programme.title: Krtek (The Little Mole)
programme.sub-title: The Little Mole and the Car
programme.desc: Krtek finds a toy car and takes it on an adventure through the forest, but pollution from the car harms his meadow. An early environmental message wrapped in gentle animation.

programme.title: The China Shop
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #41 (1934). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: Elementary, My Dear
programme.desc: A Sherlock Holmes-styled detective investigates the mystery of the fours times table. "Elementary, my dear — two times two is four, four times two is eight..." Sung by Blossom Dearie with her distinctive wispy vocal style. Part of Multiplication Rock. Teaches the fours multiplication table through a detective narrative of clue-finding and deduction.

programme.title: Funny Little Bunnies
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #43 (1934). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

programme.title: You Earned Your Diploma / Presidential Minute
programme.desc: A double feature from the 1993 revival. "You Earned Your Diploma" celebrates graduation and civic responsibility. "Presidential Minute" runs through the presidents of the United States as a rapid-fire memory exercise. A companion to the more famous "I'm Just a Bill," focusing on the structural framework rather than the legislative process. Part of America Rock. Performed by Jack Sheldon.

The train metaphor is so perfectly matched to the concept — conjunctions literally couple things together — that it became the definitive example of the series' genius. Four-time Daytime Emmy winner. programme.title: Elmer Elephant

Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips: Introduction
programme.desc: The introduction to the Scooter Computer and Mr. Chips series — the 1980s addition to Schoolhouse Rock teaching kids about personal computers. Scooter is a skateboarding kid, Mr. Chips is a friendly computer. Together they explain the digital revolution to a generation that was about to live through it. The weakest era of Schoolhouse Rock by consensus, but historically fascinating as a time capsule of early computer literacy education.

Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto — the whole tour set to a disco beat. One of the most popular Science Rock episodes, both for its earworm melody and for the sheer joy of its space animation. Pluto was still a planet. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Lynn Ahrens.

programme.title: Verb: That's What's Happening
programme.desc: A superhero called Verb flies through the city demonstrating action words. "I get my thing in action — VERB! To be, to sing, to feel, to live — VERB! That's what's happening." Zachary Sanders delivers the vocal with disco-era energy. The animation puts Verb in a cape, soaring over buildings while performing every action he names. One of the most beloved Grammar Rock episodes. Written by Bob Dorough.

programme.title: The Weather Show
programme.desc: How weather works — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and the water cycle. Sun heats the ocean, water evaporates, clouds form, rain falls, rivers flow back to the ocean, repeat. The last of the original Science Rock episodes, wrapping up the 1970s run with the biggest system of all: the atmosphere. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: I'm Just a Bill (Folk Implosion)
programme.desc: Folk Implosion (Lou Barlow of Dinosaur Jr/Sebadoh) covers the iconic civics lesson. A lo-fi indie rock version of the most famous Schoolhouse Rock song. Part of the 2002 Schoolhouse Rock Rocks! tribute compilation.

programme.title: A Victim of Gravity
programme.desc: Newton's apple, falling objects, and the universal force that keeps us stuck to the Earth. The first Science Rock episode introduces gravity through a kid who keeps dropping things and wondering why everything falls down, never up. The animation visualizes gravitational pull as an invisible hand. Part of Science Rock.

programme.title: Little Twelvetoes
programme.desc: An alien with twelve fingers and twelve toes lives on a planet where base-12 is natural. "Now if man had been born with six fingers on each hand, he'd also have twelve toes, or so the theory goes." Bob Dorough uses this sci-fi premise to teach the twelves times table while sneaking in a lesson about why we use base-10 (we have ten fingers) and how other number bases work. The most conceptually ambitious Multiplication Rock episode — it teaches multiplication AND number theory. Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: I Got Six
programme.desc: A funky soul number about the sixes times table. "I got six — that's all, and that's been my lucky number since I was very small." Grady Tate brings a warm, grooving vocal to the multiplication facts that feel the least intuitive to kids (6×7, 6×8, 6×9). Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: The Grasshopper And The Ants

programme.title: I'm Gonna Send Your Vote to College
programme.desc: The Electoral College explained. Your vote goes to college — the Electoral College — where electors cast the actual ballots for President. A revival-era America Rock episode that tackles one of the most confusing parts of American democracy. The surround-sound remix suggests this is from a later home video release. Jack Sheldon returns to voice the befuddled voter trying to understand why his vote takes a detour through 538 electors.

programme.title: Krtek (The Little Mole)

programme.desc: Krtek finds a toy car and takes it on an adventure through the forest, but pollution from the car harms his meadow. An early environmental message wrapped in gentle animation.

Sung by Blossom Dearie with her distinctive wispy vocal style. Part of Multiplication Rock. Teaches the fours multiplication table through a detective narrative of clue-finding and deduction.

programme.title: Funny Little Bunnies
programme.desc: Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies #43 (1934). Part of the complete Silly Symphonies collection (1929-1939).

"Presidential Minute" runs through the presidents of the United States as a rapid-fire memory exercise. Both are shorter, less musically ambitious than the 1970s originals, but they round out the America Rock series with a nod to civic participation beyond just knowing how government works. programme.title: The Preamble
programme.desc: The Preamble to the United States Constitution, set to music and sung in its entirety. Generations of Americans learned the Preamble not from school but from this three-minute cartoon. The melody is so effective as a mnemonic that adults who watched this as children can still sing it decades later but cannot recite it without the tune. Part of America Rock. Performed by Lynn Ahrens.

Arguably the single most culturally impactful Schoolhouse Rock episode — referenced in The Simpsons, Saturday Night Live, and countless civics classes. It taught more Americans about the legislative process than any textbook. Part of America Rock.

programme.title: The Energy Blues

One of the few Schoolhouse Rock episodes that feels explicitly political, reflecting the national anxiety of its era. Part of Science Rock. Performed by Jack Sheldon.

The easy pattern of the elevens (11, 22, 33...) makes this one of the more approachable episodes, with the animation built around a football game where the score keeps climbing by elevens. Part of Multiplication Rock. Sung by Bob Dorough.

One of the most beautiful Schoolhouse Rock episodes — the animation of the skater gliding through multiplication is genuinely graceful. Part of Multiplication Rock.

programme.title: Tax Man Max

programme.title: Son of the White Mare
programme.desc: A dying white mare tells her three sons the story of their ancestors' lost kingdom, stolen by dragons who dragged it into the Underworld. The youngest and strongest son descends through three rotating castles — copper, silver, and gold — to defeat the dragons and free three captive princesses. Marcell Jankovics' psychedelic Hungarian animation draws from ancient Hunnic, Avaric, and Magyar mythology to create something that looks like nothing else in cinema: swirling, pulsating abstract forms that shift between cosmic and cellular, painted in impossible colors. programme.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed
programme.desc: A wicked sorcerer tricks Prince Achmed into mounting a magical flying horse that carries him far from home. Across his journey, Achmed encounters the beautiful Princess Peri Banu on the island of Wak Wak, battles demons, and allies with Aladdin and the Witch of the Fiery Mountains against the sorcerer's dark magic. The oldest surviving animated feature film. Lotte Reiniger spent three years (1923–1926) creating it entirely by hand, manipulating articulated silhouette figures cut from cardboard and thin sheets of lead under a camera — a technique inspired by Indonesian Wayang shadow puppets. The result is breathtaking: intricate black figures moving against luminous colored backgrounds, every gesture precise, every scene composed like a paper theater come alive. The story weaves together episodes from One Thousand and One Nights. Accompanied by a score compiled from works by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Richard Wagner, and original compositions by Wolfgang Zeller.

programme.title: The Magic Flute
programme.desc: Ingmar Bergman's joyful, intimate film of Mozart's opera, performed in Swedish at the Drottningholm Palace Theatre — an 18th-century court theater with original hand-operated stage machinery. Prince Tamino is sent by the Queen of the Night to rescue her daughter Pamina from the High Priest Sarastro, but nothing is as it seems: the supposed villain is a wise guardian, the supposed hero must earn wisdom through trials, and the comic birdcatcher Papageno steals every scene he's in. Bergman frames the performance as a theatrical event, cutting between the stage and the audience (including a young girl whose face becomes the film's emotional anchor), and going backstage during intermission to show the performers relaxing, playing chess, reading. The result strips away operatic pomposity and reveals the human comedy underneath. Sung in Swedish translation by a cast including Josef Köstlinger, Irma Urrila, and Håkan Hagegård. Produced for Swedish television (Sveriges Television). Widely considered the finest opera film ever made.

programme.title: Peter and the Wolf
programme.desc: A boy, a bird, a duck, a cat, a grandfather, hunters, and a wolf — told entirely through Prokofiev's music and Suzie Templeton's extraordinary stop-motion animation, without a single word of narration. Peter lives behind a high wall with his overprotective grandfather. Beyond the wall is a frozen forest where a wolf hunts. When Peter's duck friend wanders outside, the wolf swallows it whole. Peter climbs the wall, enlists the bird as a decoy, and lowers a rope from a tree branch to catch the wolf by its tail. The animation is breathtaking — snow falls with real weight, the wolf's eyes glow yellow in the dark, the duck's fate is genuinely distressing. Templeton strips away the narration that usually cushions Prokofiev's fairy tale and lets the music and images do everything. The result won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film in 2008. Hänsel und Gretel
programme.desc: Humperdinck's fairy tale opera in its definitive recording: Georg Solti conducting the Vienna Philharmonic, with Edita Gruberova as Gretel and Brigitte Fassbaender as Hansel. Two children are sent into the forest to pick strawberries by their desperate mother. They get lost. They find a house made of cake and candy. The woman who lives there is a witch who eats children. What makes this opera extraordinary is that Humperdinck — Wagner's own assistant — took the full Wagnerian orchestral apparatus and pointed it at a bedtime story. The Evening Prayer, where Hansel and Gretel fall asleep in the forest and fourteen angels descend to protect them, is one of the most beautiful things in all of opera. The witch's ride on her broomstick is terrifying and hilarious. The final scene, where the gingerbread children are restored to life, is pure joy. Gruberova's silvery soprano and Fassbaender's warm mezzo are the perfect sibling pair. Solti drives the Vienna Phil with his characteristic intensity — the overture alone is worth the price of admission. Sung in German with the full forces of the Vienna State Opera.

programme.title: Allegro non Troppo
programme.desc: Bruno Bozzetto's audacious Italian answer to Fantasia — six pieces of classical music set to wildly inventive animation, ranging from slapstick comedy to devastating tragedy. A discarded Coca-Cola bottle seeds life on a barren planet to Ravel's Bolero. An aging satyr chases lost youth through Debussy's Prelude. A cat wanders through the ruins of a demolished home, remembering the family that once lived there, set to Sibelius's Valse Triste — one of the most heartbreaking sequences in the history of animation. Between segments, black-and-white live-action sequences follow the hapless fictional production crew as they attempt to stage this whole mess, starring a young Maurizio Nichetti as the put-upon animator. Disney veteran Ward Kimball used to recommend the Bolero segment to his students. The title is a musical pun: "allegro ma non troppo" means "fast, but not too much," but without the "ma," it reads as "not too happy" — which captures the film's bittersweet spirit perfectly.

programme.title: Carnival of the Animals
programme.desc: Joanna Lumley narrates Saint-Saëns' beloved musical menagerie with the London Mozart Players. Fourteen short movements, each a portrait of a different creature: the royal march of the lion, hens pecking in the barnyard, wild donkeys galloping across the steppe, tortoises performing the can-can in devastating slow motion, an elephant waltzing, kangaroos bouncing, an aquarium shimmering, a cuckoo calling from the depths of the woods, birds fluttering in an aviary, pianists practicing their scales (Saint-Saëns' wickedest joke — he classified pianists as animals), fossils dancing a xylophone danse macabre, and the sublime swan, whose cello solo is the most famous piece he ever wrote and the only movement he allowed published in his lifetime. He wrote the whole thing as a private joke for friends and suppressed it for decades, afraid it would damage his reputation as a Serious Composer. Lumley's narration threads through the movements with exactly the right mix of warmth and mischief — she knows this is music for children that adults love even more.
